(B) (i) An alternating voltage v = v₀ sin ωt is applied across a pure capacitor C. Obtain the expression for the current and show that it leads the voltage by π/2. Show that the average power over a cycle is zero. [3m]
(ii) A 50 μF capacitor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find its reactance and the rms and peak values of the current. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) q = Cv = Cv₀ sin ωt → i = dq/dt = ωCv₀ cos ωt = i₀ sin(ωt + π/2), with i₀ = v₀/X_C and X_C = 1/(ωC). [1]
So the current reaches its maximum a quarter cycle before the voltage: it leads by π/2. [1]
P_av = V_rms I_rms cos(π/2) = 0 (the capacitor stores energy for a quarter cycle and returns it in the next). [1]
(ii) X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 50×10⁻⁶) ≈ 63.7 Ω. [1]
I_rms = 220/63.7 ≈ 3.46 A; I₀ = √2 × 3.46 ≈ 4.89 A. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) With a labelled diagram, describe a Cassegrain reflecting telescope. Give two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope. [3m]
(ii) The objective mirror of a reflecting telescope has a radius of curvature of 4 m and the eyepiece has a focal length of 2 cm. Find the magnifying power in normal adjustment. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Diagram: a large concave (paraboloidal) primary mirror with a hole at its centre; a small convex secondary mirror placed before the primary's focus reflects the converging rays back through the hole to form the image, which is viewed with an eyepiece behind the primary. [2]
Advantages (any two): no chromatic aberration (reflection does not depend on wavelength); paraboloidal mirror removes spherical aberration; a mirror needs support only at its back, so very large apertures are possible (more light, better resolution); cheaper to make a large mirror than a large lens. [1]
(ii) f₀ = R/2 = 2 m = 200 cm; m = f₀/f_e = 200/2 = 100. [2]
items.orq:
(B) (i) What are coherent sources? Two coherent waves of equal amplitude a, with phase difference φ, superpose at a point. Show that the resultant intensity is I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2), where I₀ is the intensity of each wave, and write the conditions for constructive and destructive interference. [3m]
(ii) In a Young's double-slit experiment the intensity at the central maximum is I_max. Find the intensity at points where the path difference is (a) λ/4, (b) λ/3. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a constant (time-independent) phase difference. [½]
y₁ = a cos ωt, y₂ = a cos(ωt + φ) → y = 2a cos(φ/2) cos(ωt + φ/2); resultant amplitude 2a cos(φ/2). [1]
Intensity ∝ amplitude²: I = 4a² cos²(φ/2) = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2). [½]
Constructive: φ = 2nπ (path difference nλ) → I = 4I₀; destructive: φ = (2n + 1)π (path difference (n + ½)λ) → I = 0. [1]
(ii) I_max = 4I₀, so I = I_max cos²(φ/2) with φ = (2π/λ) × path difference. [½]
(a) φ = π/2 → I = I_max cos²45° = I_max/2. [½]
(b) φ = 2π/3 → I = I_max cos²60° = I_max/4. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor. Hence show that the energy density of the electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is ½ε₀E². [3m]
(ii) A parallel plate air capacitor has plates of area 0.04 m² separated by 2 mm and is connected to a 100 V supply. Find its capacitance, the energy stored and the energy density between the plates. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) To transfer charge dq when the capacitor already has charge q (p.d. q/C), work dW = (q/C)dq. W = ∫₀^Q (q/C)dq = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV, stored as electric potential energy. [1½]
For a parallel plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d and V = Ed: U = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)² = ½ε₀E²(Ad). Since Ad is the volume between the plates, energy density u = ½ε₀E². [1½]
(ii) C = ε₀A/d = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.04/0.002 = 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ F = 177 pF; U = ½CV² = ½ × 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ × 100² ≈ 8.85×10⁻⁷ J. [1]
E = V/d = 5×10⁴ V/m; u = ½ × 8.85×10⁻¹² × (5×10⁴)² ≈ 1.1×10⁻² J/m³ (check: u × volume = 0.011 × 8×10⁻⁵ ≈ 8.85×10⁻⁷ J). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Derive an expression for the torque on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field. Hence obtain the expression for the potential energy of the dipole, U = −pE cos θ. [3m]
(ii) An electric dipole of moment 2×10⁻⁸ C m is in a uniform field of 5×10⁴ N/C. Find the torque when its axis is perpendicular to the field, and the work done in turning it from the position of stable equilibrium to that of unstable equilibrium. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Forces +qE and −qE act on the charges (separation 2a): net force zero, but they form a couple. Perpendicular distance between the lines of action = 2a sin θ, so τ = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ, i.e. τ = p × E. [1½]
Work done in rotating the dipole from θ₀ to θ: W = ∫pE sin θ dθ = pE(cos θ₀ − cos θ). Taking U = 0 at θ₀ = 90°: U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E. [1½]
(ii) τ = pE sin 90° = 2×10⁻⁸ × 5×10⁴ = 1×10⁻³ N m. [1]
Stable (θ = 0°) to unstable (θ = 180°): W = pE(cos 0° − cos 180°) = 2pE = 2×10⁻³ J. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Explain the principle and working of a moving-coil galvanometer. Why is the magnetic field made radial, and why is a soft-iron core used? Define its current sensitivity. [3m]
(ii) A galvanometer coil has 100 turns, each of area 2 cm², and hangs in a radial field of 0.25 T. The torsional constant of the suspension is 1×10⁻⁶ N m per degree. Find the deflection for a current of 1 mA and the current sensitivity. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Principle: a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque τ = NIAB. The coil turns until this is balanced by the restoring torque kφ of the spring: NIAB = kφ → φ = (NAB/k)I, so deflection ∝ current. [1]
The concave pole pieces and the soft-iron cylindrical core make the field radial and stronger, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B (sin 90° = 1) and the scale is linear; the core also increases the field (and sensitivity). [1]
Current sensitivity = φ/I = NAB/k (deflection per unit current). [1]
(ii) τ = NIAB = 100 × 1×10⁻³ × 2×10⁻⁴ × 0.25 = 5×10⁻⁶ N m; φ = τ/k = 5×10⁻⁶/1×10⁻⁶ = 5°. [1]
Current sensitivity = 5° per mA (5×10³ degree per ampere). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Obtain an expression for the average power dissipated in a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source. Define power factor and explain the term wattless current. [3m]
(ii) In an AC circuit the rms voltage is 220 V and the rms current is 5 A, the current lagging the voltage by 60°. Find the average power consumed and the wattless component of the current. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) v = v₀ sin ωt, i = i₀ sin(ωt − φ). Instantaneous power p = vi = v₀i₀ sin ωt sin(ωt − φ) = (v₀i₀/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so P_av = (v₀i₀/2) cos φ = V_rms I_rms cos φ. [1½]
Power factor = cos φ = R/Z. [½]
Wattless current: the component of current I_rms sin φ, perpendicular (90° out of phase) to the voltage; it contributes zero average power. [1]
(ii) P = 220 × 5 × cos 60° = 550 W. [1]
Wattless component = I_rms sin 60° = 5 × 0.866 ≈ 4.33 A. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) A spherical surface of radius of curvature R separates a rarer medium (refractive index μ₁) from a denser medium (μ₂). Derive the relation μ₂/v − μ₁/u = (μ₂ − μ₁)/R for a point object on the principal axis in the rarer medium (real image in the denser medium). [3m]
(ii) One end of a long glass rod (μ = 1.5) is ground into a convex hemispherical surface of radius 6 cm. An object is placed in air on the axis, 30 cm from this surface. Find the position of the image. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Ray from O strikes the surface at N and refracts towards the normal NC to meet the axis at I. For small angles: i = α + γ, r = γ − β, with α ≈ MN/OM, β ≈ MN/MI, γ ≈ MN/MC. [1]
Snell's law for small angles: μ₁i = μ₂r → μ₁(α + γ) = μ₂(γ − β). [1]
Substituting: μ₁/OM + μ₂/MI = (μ₂ − μ₁)/MC. With the sign convention OM = −u, MI = +v, MC = +R: μ₂/v − μ₁/u = (μ₂ − μ₁)/R. [1]
(ii) μ₁ = 1, μ₂ = 1.5, u = −30 cm, R = +6 cm: 1.5/v = 0.5/6 + 1/(−30) = 0.0833 − 0.0333 = 0.05. [1]
v = 1.5/0.05 = +30 cm: a real image forms inside the rod, 30 cm from the surface. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Draw the graph of angle of deviation δ against angle of incidence i for a prism. Derive the relation μ = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2), where δ_m is the angle of minimum deviation. [3m]
(ii) A ray passes through a prism of angle 60° and refractive index 1.6 in the position of minimum deviation. Find the angle of incidence and the angle of minimum deviation. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Graph: δ first decreases as i increases, reaches a minimum δ_m, then increases (U-shaped curve); for every δ other than δ_m there are two values of i. [1]
For any ray: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A. At minimum deviation i = e and r₁ = r₂ = r, so r = A/2 and i = (A + δ_m)/2. [1]
μ = sin i/sin r = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2). [1]
(ii) r = 30°; sin i = 1.6 × sin 30° = 0.8 → i ≈ 53.1°. [1]
δ_m = 2i − A = 106.3° − 60° ≈ 46.3°. [1]
